data.title: 13D Filings — Barrons.com
data.description:
These disclosures are from 13Ds filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. 13Ds are filed within 10 days of an entity's attaining more than 5% in any class of a company's securities. Subsequent changes in holdings or intentions must be reported in amended filings. This material is from Oct. 29 through Nov. 4, 2026. Source: VerityData

Increases in Holdings

Group 1 Automotive (GPI) Conifer Management raised its stake in the automotive retailer to 2,012,290 shares. Conifer Management did so through the purchase of 171,592 Group 1 Automotive shares from Sept. 30 through Oct. 26 at per share prices ranging from $226 to $249.84. Following the latest purchases, Conifer Management continues to own a 16.9% stake in Group 1 Automotive's outstanding stock. Shares of Group 1 Automotive have lost roughly 30.1% of their value since the beginning of this year.

Corebridge Financial (CRBG) Nippon Life Insurance raised its stake in the retirement solutions and insurance provider to 131,262,715 shares. Nippon Life did so through the purchase of 4,658,665 Corebridge Financial shares from Oct. 5 through Oct. 23 at per share prices ranging from $32.28 to $35.58. This comes after Corebridge Financial shareholders approved a definitive merger with Equitable Holdings back in July that is expected to close by year end. Following the latest purchases, Nippon Life owns a 29.4% stake in Corebridge Financial's outstanding stock. Shares of Corebridge Financial have gained approximately 19.4% in value in 2026.

Nano Dimension (NNDM) Murchinson raised its stake in the additive manufacturing company to 20,416,500 shares. Murchinson did so through the purchase of 416,500 Nano Dimension shares from Sept. 3 through Sept. 4 at per share prices of $1.60 to $1.62. Following the latest purchases, Murchinson owns a 10.1% stake in Nano Dimension's outstanding stock. Shares of Nano Dimension have lost roughly 15.1% of their value in 2026.

Decreases in Holdings

Quanex Building Products (NX) Teleios Capital Partners lowered its stake in the building products components maker to 4,022,113 shares. Teleios Capital Partners did so through the sale of 229,766 Quanex Building Products shares from Oct. 22 through Oct. 26 at per share prices ranging from $19.50 to $21.12. Following the latest sales, Teleios Capital Partners continues to own an 8.8% stake in Quanex Building Products' outstanding stock. Shares of Quanex Building Products have gained roughly 45.8% in value in 2026.

American Outdoor Brands (AOUT) Engine Capital lowered its stake in the outdoor products company to 545,324 shares. Engine Capital did so through the sale of 111,005 American Outdoor Brands shares from Sept. 29 through Oct. 7 at per share prices ranging from $16.05 to $16.96. Following the latest sales, Engine Capital continues to own a 4.3% stake in American Outdoor Brands' outstanding stock, placing Engine Capital below the 5% threshold that would require it to report further sales. Shares of American Outdoor Brands have gained roughly 124.6% in value since the beginning of this year.

data.title: IMF's Georgieva says any slowdown in AI-driven growth would be factor for central banks
data.description:
By Andrea Shalal

Central bankers around the world would need to consider any slowdown in AI-driven growth as they assess steps in their fight against inflation, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Friday.

Georgieva said concerns about dependence on the AI investment boom and high valuations were impacting markets around the world.

"Things are going up and down, and this is likely to continue," she told an audience at IMF headquarters in Washington, adding that the volatility would complicate the job of central banks at a time when risks to price stability had been growing.

A steep rout in technology stocks on Thursday rippled through markets on fears that the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections would increase regulatory scrutiny of AI and slow the data center build-out, sending investors to the safety of bonds.

The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worry about return on massive spending on AI-related infrastructure, with the meltdown spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

Georgieva said the AI investment boom was lifting growth in some countries, helping to offset a negative oil-supply shock triggered by the war in the Middle East, but it was also adding to inflationary pressures and financial stability concerns.

The IMF last month flagged significant growth and financial stability risks from a potential ending of the AI investment boom, among other factors, including a prolonged Middle East war. At the time, it warned that a steep drop in AI investment could lead to a sharp fall ⁠in asset prices, ultimately cutting global GDP by 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output.

Georgieva did not repeat the downside forecast on Friday, but acknowledged the recent market volatility.

"Should there be a slowdown in the AI-driven growth impulse, it would need to be factored in as central banks assess the necessary steps in the fight against stubborn inflation," she said.

Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of the US Congress in January, Reuters reported on Friday, citing congressional aides and advocates.

That would mark ​a sharp shift from the Republican-led Congress, where lawmakers largely focused on promoting AI development and declined to pass legislation restricting the ‌technology.

data.title: Alaska high court revives opioid lawsuit against pharmacy operators
data.description:
By Nate Raymond

Alaska's top court ruled on Friday that the state can pursue a lawsuit alleging pharmacies operated by Albertsons and Kroger helped fuel the opioid epidemic by failing to meet their obligations when dispensing addictive painkillers.

The Alaska Supreme Court reversed a judge's 2024 ruling dismissing the case brought by the state's attorney general against the operators of the Safeway and Fred Meyer grocery chains, finding the state had plausibly alleged the pharmacies' actions created a public nuisance.

"Taking the State’s allegations as true, we hold that the pharmacies’ failure to fulfill their legal obligations when dispensing opioids unreasonably interfered with public rights protected by the common law," Justice Jude Pate wrote for the unanimous five-justice court.

The Alaska Department of Law in a statement welcomed the ruling and said it looked forward to the case moving forward in the coming months.

Spokespeople for Albertsons and Kroger did not respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit is among thousands brought by states and local governments seeking to hold pharmaceutical manufacturers, drug distributors and pharmacies responsible for a deadly opioid epidemic that for years ravaged the US.

In Alaska, the number of drug overdose deaths climbed steadily over the decade leading up to the state suing in 2022, according to the state. That included a 68% increase from 2020 to 2021.

Friday's ruling came a day after a judge in Washington state ordered Albertsons to pay $900 million in a similar case by that state's attorney general, who had opted to take the company to trial rather than join a $774 million nationwide settlement the company announced in April to resolve the cases against it.

Kroger in 2023 agreed to pay as much as $1.4 billion to resolve similar cases nationwide against it.

Alaska did not settle with those companies, though it did settle with Walgreens and Walmart, which were also defendants in the 2022 lawsuit. The state alleged the companies' pharmacies failed to monitor and report suspicious opioid prescriptions.

In 2024, a judge dismissed the state's public nuisance and consumer protection claims, prompting the appeal.

The Alaska Supreme Court largely agreed that most of the state's claims under its consumer protection statute could not be pursued, saying that under state law, the pharmacies could not be sued under that statute if their actions were already subject to Alaska's controlled substances regulations.

But it said Alaska could pursue a claim that the pharmacies misled the public about meeting their legal obligations and seek remedies for harms allegedly caused by the public nuisance the state alleges the companies created.

If the companies are found liable on that claim, the state contends they should be forced to address, or abate, the public nuisance by providing addiction treatment to patients and making naloxone widely available.

"Courts have recognized that similar allegations against opioid manufacturers and distributors are sufficient to constitute an interference with the rights to public health and public safety," Pate wrote.

The case is State of Alaska v Albertsons Companies, et al, Alaska Supreme Court, No. S-19048.

For Alaska: Laura Fox of the Alaska Department of Law

For Albertsons: Frank Citera of Greenberg Traurig

For Kroger: Rebecca Hozubin of Hozubin Moberly & Associates
